n: Four documents, all dated Tuesday, all from GitHub's changelog. The first puts evals into public preview for its coding assistant. It defines an eval as a repeatable test for AI behavior: you give an agent a realistic task, describe what a good result looks like, and check both the result and how the agent got there. It says AI output can change from one run to the next, so you run the same test again after you change your setup. The second lets the assistant's security review run the company's secret scanning on code changes before they merge, to catch passwords and keys left in the code. It is a public preview and it is off until you turn it on. The third lets the assistant control a web browser through a Chrome extension, also in public preview. The fourth lets large organizations stream the assistant's agent activity, including prompts, responses and tool calls, into a Microsoft control plane where administrators can review it. What it means for your work: one good answer does not tell you an AI setup works. Keep three or four real tasks from your own week, write down what good looks like for each, and run them again every time you change your instructions or your tools.
